title: Your AI Teaching Toolkit
author: Jeremy Caplan
summary: Jeremy Caplan's Wonder Tools newsletter offers K-12 teachers an eleven-prompt library for using general AI assistants like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to cut down on the uncompensated hours teachers spend on prep and administrative work. Rather than treating AI as a magic fix, Caplan frames it as a way to offload tedious drafting so teachers can redirect energy toward what only a human teacher can do, while insisting the teacher must iterate on and adapt every output rather than using it as-is. Each prompt in the collection targets a specific recurring teaching task, from opening-class "bell ringers" to rubric-building to auditing a lesson plan for accessibility blind spots, and each comes with a fill-in-the-blank template. The piece closes by grounding the whole exercise in RAND survey data on teacher overwork and underpay, arguing AI's real value is time reclaimed, not compensation restored.
points: Caplan's central discipline is to insist teachers 'retain agency' by treating every AI output as a draft to adapt, not a finished product to use as-is, explicitly naming the risk of cognitive offloading in the Differentiation Prompt section.

The 'Bad Example Generator' repurposes AI's fluency for generating plausible wrong answers as a pedagogical tool, letting teachers show common errors without the ethical problem of using an actual student's weak work.

The 'Blind Spot Audit' turns AI into a stand-in for peer feedback teachers rarely have time to seek, specifically probing for unconscious bias, unclear instructions, and non-inclusive examples in existing lesson materials.

Caplan frames the entire toolkit against RAND data showing only 24% of teachers are satisfied with their hours and 66% call their base salary inadequate, positioning AI as time-relief rather than a substitute for structural compensation fixes.
quotes: The average K-12 teacher works 49 hours a week. About a quarter of that time is uncompensated. Most teachers I know didn't become educators to spend evenings generating quiz questions, rewriting instructions, or filling out administrative paperwork.

It helps to iterate on AI output with follow-up prompts. Ask for more specificity or detail. Adapt the response for your students. Don't use it as is. Part of retaining your agency in the process is making sure you build on whatever outputs an assistant generates.

Showing students examples of mistakes can help them avoid those pitfalls. But you can't embarrass students by showing examples of their weakest work. Fortunately, AI assistants are excellent example generators.
Tip: make sure your differentiated materials remain anchored in your own ideas and teaching goals. There's a risk of cognitive offloading, where you start letting the AI make decisions for you.
In a national survey by the RAND Corporation, just 24% of teachers reported being satisfied with their total weekly hours worked, and 66% said their base salary was inadequate.
AI tools won't make up for unfair compensation. But they can help us strengthen how we serve our students while we make time for the rest of our lives.
